entries.70b23bb45f67be2a8ee3bbd33044931acc758868: <chapter n="1" osisID="Obad.1" sID="Obad.1"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> is the shortest of all the books of the Old Testament, the least of those tribes, and yet is not to be passed by, or thought meanly of, for this penny has Cæsar's image and superscription upon it; it is stamped with a divine authority. There may appear much of God in a short sermon, in a little book; and much good may be done by it, <hi type="italic">multum in parvo—much in a little.</hi> Mr. Norris says, "If angels were to write books, we should have few folios." That may be very precious which is not voluminous. This book is entitled, <hi type="italic">The Vision of Obadiah.</hi> Who this Obadiah was does not appear from any other scripture. Some of the ancients imagined him to be the same with that Obadiah that was steward to Ahab's household (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.3">1 Kings xviii. 3</reference>); and, if so, he that hid and fed the prophets had indeed a prophet's reward, when he was himself made a prophet. But that is a conjecture which has no ground. This Obadiah, it is probable, was of a later date, some think contemporary with Hosea, Joel, and Amos; others think he lived about the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, when the children of Edom so barbarously triumphed in that destruction. However, what he wrote was what he saw; it is his <hi type="italic">vision.</hi> Probably there was much more which he was divinely inspired to speak, but this is all he was inspired to write; and all he writes is concerning Edom. It is a foolish fancy of some of the Jews that because he prophesies only concerning Edom he was himself an Edomite by birth, but a proselyte to the Jewish religion. Other prophets prophesied against Edom, and some of them seem to have borrowed from him in their predictions against Edom, as <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jer. xlix. 7,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12">Ezek. xxv. 12</reference>, &c. Out of the mouth of these two or three witnesses every word will be established. <div eID="gen20263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20264" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20265" type="x-p"/> This book is wholly concerning Edom, a nation nearly allied and near adjoining to Israel, and yet an enemy to the seed of Jacob, inheriting the enmity of their father Esau to Jacob. Now here we have, after the preface, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.1">ver. 1</reference>. I. Threatenings against Edom, 1. That their pride should be humbled, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.2-Obad.1.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. 2. That their wealth should be plundered, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.5-Obad.1.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. 3. That their wisdom should be infatuated, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.8-Obad.1.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. 4. That their spiteful behaviour towards God's Israel should be avenged, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.10-Obad.1.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. II. Gracious promises to Israel; that they shall be restored and reformed, and shall be victorious over the Edomites, and become masters of their land and the lands of others of their neighbours (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.17-Obad.1.20">ver. 17-20</reference>), and that the kingdom of the Messiah shall be set up by the bringing in of the great salvation, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.21">ver. 21</reference>.
entries.ac77121b0bd2b43c58a9e637144833246ad31ef0: <div eID="gen20265" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20264" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Edom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen20266" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The vision of Obadiah. Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> concerning Edom; We have heard a rumour from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and an ambassador is sent among the heathen, Arise ye, and let us rise up against her in battle. <hi type="super">2</hi> Behold, I have made thee small among the heathen: thou art greatly despised. <hi type="super">3</hi> The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation <hi type="italic">is</hi> high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground? <hi type="super">4</hi> Though thou exalt <hi type="italic">thyself</hi> as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grape-gatherers came to thee, would they not leave <hi type="italic">some</hi> grapes? <hi type="super">6</hi> How are <hi type="italic">the things</hi> of Esau searched out! <hi type="italic">how</hi> are his hidden things sought up! <hi type="super">7</hi> All the men of thy confederacy have brought thee <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the border: the men that were at peace with thee have deceived thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> prevailed against thee; <hi type="italic">they that eat</hi> thy bread have laid a wound under thee: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none understanding in him. <hi type="super">8</hi> Shall I not in that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , even destroy the wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> out of Edom, and understanding out of the mount of Esau? <hi type="super">9</hi> And thy mighty <hi type="italic">men,</hi> O Teman, shall be dismayed, to the end that every one of the mount of Esau may be cut off by slaughter. <div eID="gen20266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20267" type="x-p"/> Edom is the nation against which this prophecy is levelled, and which, some think, is put for all the enemies of Israel, that shall be brought down first or last. The rabbin by Edom understand Rome. Rome Christians they understand it of, and have an implacable enmity to it a such; but, if we understand it of Rome antichristian, we shall find the passages of it applicable enough. And though Edom was mortified in the times of the Maccabees, as it had been before by Jehoshaphat, yet its destruction seems to have been typical, as their father Esau's rejection, and to have had further reference to the destruction of the enemies of the gospel-church; for so shall all God's enemies perish; and we find (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Isa. xxxiv. 5</reference>) the <hi type="italic">sword of the Lord</hi> coming down <hi type="italic">upon Idumea,</hi> to signify the general day of God's recompences for the controversy of Zion, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.8">v. 8</reference>. Some have well observed that it could not but be a great temptation to the people of Israel, when they saw themselves, who were the children of beloved Jacob, in trouble, and the Edomites, not only prospering, but triumphing over them in their troubles; and therefore God gives them a prospect of the destruction of Edom, which should be total and final, and of a happy issue of their own correction. Now we may observe here, <div eID="gen20267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20268" type="x-p"/> I. A declaration of war against Edom, (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We have heard a rumour,</hi> or rather <hi type="italic">an order, from the Lord,</hi> the God of hosts; he has given the word of command; it is his counsel and decree, which can neither be reversed nor resisted, that all who do mischief to his people shall certainly bring mischief upon themselves. We have heard a report that God is raised up out of his holy habitation, and is preparing his throne for judgment; and <hi type="italic">an ambassador is sent among the heathen,</hi>" a <hi type="italic">herald</hi> rather, some minister or messenger of Providence, to alarm the nations, or the Lord's prophets, who gave each nation its burden. Those whom God employs cry to each other, <hi type="italic">Arise ye,</hi> stir up yourselves and one another, and let <hi type="italic">us rise up against Edom in battle.</hi> The confederate forces under Nebuchadnezzar thus animate themselves and one another to make a descent upon that country: <hi type="italic">Gather yourselves together, and come against her;</hi> so it is in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.14">Jer. xlix. 14</reference>. Note, When God has bloody work to do among the enemies of his church he will find out and fit up both hands and hearts to do it. <div eID="gen20268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20269" type="x-p"/> II. A prediction of the success of that war. Edom shall certainly be subdued, and spoiled, and brought down; for all her confidences shall fail her and stand her in no stead, and in like manner shall all the enemies of God's church be disappointed in those things which they stayed themselves upon. <div eID="gen20269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20270" type="x-p"/> 1. Do they depend upon their grandeur, the figure they make among the nations, their influence upon them, and interest in them? That shall dwindle (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold, I have made thee small among the heathen,</hi> so that none of thy neighbours will court thy friendship, or court an alliance with thee; <hi type="italic">thou art greatly despised</hi> among them, and looked upon with contempt, as an infatuated and unfaithful nation." And thus (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.3">v. 3</reference>) <hi type="italic">the pride of thy heart has deceived thee.</hi> Note, (1.) Those that think well of themselves are apt to fancy that others think well of them too; but, when they come to make trial of them, they will find themselves mistaken, and thus their pride deceives them and by it slays them. (2.) God can easily lay those low that have magnified and exalted themselves, and will find out a way to do it, for he <hi type="italic">resists the proud;</hi> and we often see those small and greatly despised who once looked very big and were greatly caressed and admired. <div eID="gen20270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20271" type="x-p"/> 2. Do they depend upon the fortifications of their country, both by nature and art, and glory in the advantages they have thereby? Those also shall deceive them. They <hi type="italic">dwelt in the clefts of the rock,</hi> as an eagle in her nest, and their <hi type="italic">habitation</hi> was <hi type="italic">high,</hi> not only exalted above their neighbours, which was the matter of their pride, but fortified against their enemies, which was the matter of their security, so high as to be out of the reach of danger. Now observe, (1.) What Edom says in the pride of his heart: <hi type="italic">Who shall bring me down to the ground?</hi> He speaks with a confidence of his own strength, and a contempt of God's judgments, as if almighty power itself could not overpower him. As for <hi type="italic">all his enemies,</hi> even God himself, he <hi type="italic">puffs at them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.5">Ps. x. 5</reference>), sets them all at defiance. Their father Esau had <hi type="italic">sold his birthright,</hi> and yet they lifted up themselves, as if to them had still pertained the <hi type="italic">excellency of dignity and power.</hi> Many forfeit their privileges, and yet boast of them. Because Edom is high and lifted up, he imagines none can bring him down. Note, Carnal security is a sin that most easily besets men in the day of their pomp, power, and prosperity, and does, as much as any thing, both ripen men for ruin and aggravate it when it comes. (2.) What God says to this, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.4">v. 4</reference>. If men will dare to challenge Omnipotence, their challenge shall be taken up: <hi type="italic">Who shall bring me down?</hi> says Edom. "<hi type="italic">I will,</hi>" says God. "<hi type="italic">Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle</hi> that soars high and builds high, nay, <hi type="italic">though thou set thy nest among stars,</hi> higher than ever any eagle flew, it is but in thy own imagination, and <hi type="italic">thence will I bring thee down.</hi>" This we had <reference osisRef="Jer.49.15-Jer.49.16">Jer. xlix. 15, 16</reference>. Note, Sinners will certainly be made ashamed of their pride and security of their pride when it has a fall and of their security when their confidences fail their expectation. <div eID="gen20271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20272" type="x-p"/> 3. Do they depend upon their wealth and treasure, the abundance of which is looked upon as the sinews of war? Is their money their defence? Is that their strong city? It is so only in their own conceit, for it shall rather expose them than protect them; it shall be made a prey to the enemy, and they for the sake of it, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.5-Obad.1.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Much to this purport we had <reference osisRef="Jer.49.9-Jer.49.10">Jer. xlix. 9, 10</reference>. Only here comes in, in a parenthesis, <hi type="italic">How art thou cut off!</hi> thou and all thy stores. The prophet foretels it, but laments it, that the thread of their prosperity was cut off. How art thou fallen, and how great is thy fall! <hi type="italic">How art thou stupefied!</hi> so the Chaldee words it. How senseless art thou under these desolating judgments, as if they were but common strokes! But he shows that it should be an utter ruin, not a usual calamity; for, (1.) It is indeed a usual calamity for those that have wealth to have it stolen, and to lose a little out of their great deal. <hi type="italic">Thieves come to them</hi> (for where the carcase is, there will the birds of prey be gathered together), <hi type="italic">robbers come by night,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">steal till they have enough,</hi> what they have occasion for, what they have a mind for; they steal no more than they think they can carry away, and out of a great stock it is scarcely missed. Those that rob orchards, or vineyards, carry off what they think fit; but they <hi type="italic">leave some grapes,</hi> some fruit for the owner, who easily bears his loss perhaps and soon recruits it. But, (2.) It shall not be so with Edom; his wealth shall all be taken away, and nothing shall escape the hands of the destroying army, not that which is most precious and valuable, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">How are the things of Esau,</hi> the things he sets his heart upon and places his happiness in, his good things, his best things, how are these things, which were so carefully treasured up and concealed, now <hi type="italic">searched out</hi> by the enemy and seized! <hi type="italic">How are the hidden things,</hi> his hidden treasures, plundered, rifled, and <hi type="italic">sought up!</hi> His hoards, that had not see the light for many years, are now a spoil to the enemy. Note, Treasures on earth, though ever so fast locked up and ever so artfully hidden, cannot be so safely laid up but that thieves may break through and steal; it is therefore our wisdom to <hi type="italic">lay up for ourselves treasures in heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen20272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20273" type="x-p"/> 4. Do they depend upon their alliances with neighbouring states and potentates? Those also shall fail them (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.7">v. 7</reference>): "The <hi type="italic">men of thy confederacy,</hi> all of them, the Ammonites and Moabites, and other thy high allies that were at <hi type="italic">peace with thee,</hi> that entered into a league offensive and defensive with thee, that solemnly engaged not only to do thee no hurt, but to do thee all the service the could, <hi type="italic">did eat thy bread,</hi> were magnificently treated and entertained by thee, lived upon thee; their soldiers had free quarter in thy country, and took pay as thy auxiliaries; they <hi type="italic">brought thee even to the border</hi> of thy land, were very respectful to thy ambassadors, and brought them on their way home, even to the utmost limits of their country; they seemed forward to serve thee with their forces when thou hadst occasion for them, and came along with thee <hi type="italic">to the border,</hi> till thou wast just ready to engage the invading enemy; but then," (1.) "They had <hi type="italic">deceived thee;</hi> they flew back and retreated when thou wast in extremity, and proved as a broken reed to the traveller that is weary, and as the brooks in summer to the traveller that is thirsty; they bear no weight, yield no relief." Nay, (2.) "They have <hi type="italic">prevailed against thee;</hi> they were too hard for thee in the treaty imposed upon thee, and by cheating thee ruined thee, brought thee into danger, and there left thee an easy prey to thy enemy." Note, Those that make flesh their arm arm it against them. Yet this was not the worst. (3.) "They have <hi type="italic">laid a wound under thee;</hi> that is, they have laid that under thee for a stay and support, for a foundation to rely on, for a pillow to repose on, which will prove a wound to thee; not as thorns only, but as swords." If God lay under us the arms of his power and love, these will be firm and easy under us; the God of our covenant will never deceive us. But if we trust to <hi type="italic">the men of our confederacy,</hi> and what they will lay under us, it may prove to us a <hi type="italic">wound</hi> and <hi type="italic">dishonour.</hi> And observe the just censure here passed upon Edom for trusting to those who thus played tricks with him: "<hi type="italic">There is no understanding in him,</hi> or else he would never have put it into their power to betray him by putting such a confidence in them." Note, Those show they have no understanding in them who, when they are encouraged to trust in the Creator, put a cheat upon themselves by reposing a confidence in the creature. <div eID="gen20273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20274" type="x-p"/> 5. Do they depend upon the politics of their counsellors? These shall fail them, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.8">v. 8</reference>. Edom had been famous for great statesmen, men of learning and experience, that sat at the help of government, and were masters of all the arts of management, that in all treaties used to outwit their neighbours; but now the <hi type="italic">counsellors</hi> have become <hi type="italic">fools,</hi> and the wise God makes them so: <hi type="italic">Shall I not in that day destroy the wise men out of Edom?</hi> As men they shall fall by the sword in common with others (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">Ps. xlix. 10</reference>), and their wisdom shall not secure them; as wise men they shall be infatuated in all their counsels; their best-laid designs shall be baffled, their measures broken, and those very projects by which they thought to establish themselves and the public interests shall be the ruin of both. Thus <hi type="italic">wisdom perishes from Teman,</hi> as it is in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jer. xlix. 7</reference>. This was, (1.) The just punishment of their folly in trusting to an arm of flesh: <hi type="italic">There is no understanding in them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Obad.1.7">v. 7</reference>. They have not sense to trust in a living God, and a God of truth, but put confidence in men that are frail, fickle, and false; and therefore God will <hi type="italic">destroy their understanding.</hi> Note, God will justly deny those understanding to keep out of the way of danger that will not use their understanding to keep out of the way of sin. He that will be foolish, let him be foolish still. (2.) It was the forerunner of their destruction. A nation is certainly marked for ruin when God hides the things that belong to its peace from the eyes of those that are entrusted with its counsels. <hi type="italic">Quos Deus vult perdere, eos dementat—God infatuates those whom he designs to destroy.</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.17">Job xii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen20274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20275" type="x-p"/> 6. Do they depend upon the strength and courage of their soldiers? They are not only able-bodied, but men of spirit and courage, that can face an enemy and stand their ground; but now (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thy mighty men, O Teman! shall be dismayed;</hi> their courage shall fail them, <hi type="italic">to the end that every one of the mount of Esau may be cut off by slaughter,</hi> and none escape. The weak, and feeble, and unarmed must fall of course into the hand of the destroyer when the <hi type="italic">mighty men are dismayed,</hi> and not only lose the day, but lose their lives, because they have lost their spirit. <hi type="italic">Howl, fir-trees, if the cedars be shaken.</hi> Note, The death or disuniting of the mighty often proves the death and destruction of the many; and it is in vain to depend upon mighty men for our protection if we have not an almighty God for us, much less if we have an almighty God against us.
entries.3a25d2b41c5bbb8cea67b72b6eae19fdfcd8c657: <div eID="gen20275" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Guilt of Edom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen20276" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> For <hi type="italic">thy</hi> violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever. <hi type="super">11</hi> In the day that thou stoodest on the other side, in the day that the strangers carried away captive his forces, and foreigners entered into his gates, and cast lots upon Jerusalem, even thou <hi type="italic">wast</hi> as one of them. <hi type="super">12</hi> But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou shouldest not have entered into the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; yea, thou shouldest not have looked on their affliction in the day of their calamity, nor have laid <hi type="italic">hands</hi> on their substance in the day of their calamity; <hi type="super">14</hi> Neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape; neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress. <hi type="super">15</hi> For the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> near upon all the heathen: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head. <hi type="super">16</hi> For as ye have drunk upon my holy mountain, <hi type="italic">so</hi> shall all the heathen drink continually, yea, they shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been. <div eID="gen20276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20277" type="x-p"/> When we have read Edom's doom, no less than utter ruin, it is natural to ask, <hi type="italic">Why, what evil has he done?</hi> What is the ground of God's controversy with him? Many things, no doubt, were amiss in Edom; they were a sinful people, and <hi type="italic">a people laden with iniquity.</hi> But that one single crime which is laid to their charge, as filling their measure and bringing this ruin upon them, that for which they here stand indicted, of which they are convicted, and for which they are condemned, is the injury they had done to the people of God (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.10">v. 10</reference>): "It is <hi type="italic">for thy violence against thy brother Jacob,</hi> that ancient and hereditary grudge which thou hast borne to the people of Israel, that all this <hi type="italic">shame shall cover thee</hi> and <hi type="italic">thou shalt be cut off for ever.</hi>" Note, Injuries to men are affronts to God, the righteous God, that loveth righteousness and hateth wickedness; and, as the Judge of all the earth, he will give redress to those that suffer wrong and take vengeance on those that do wrong. All violence, all <hi type="italic">unrighteousness, is sin;</hi> but it is a great aggravation of the violence if it be done either, 1. Against any of our own people; it is violence <hi type="italic">against thy brother,</hi> thy near relation, to whom thou shouldst be a <hi type="italic">goël—a redeemer,</hi> whom it is thy duty to right if others wronged him; how wicked is it then for thee thyself to wrong him! Thou <hi type="italic">slanderest</hi> and abusest <hi type="italic">thy own mother's son;</hi> this makes the sin <hi type="italic">exceedingly sinful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.20">Ps. l. 20</reference>. Or, 2. Much more if it be done against any of God's people; "it is thy brother Jacob that is in covenant with God, and dear to him. Thou hatest him whom God has loved, and because God espouses and will plead with jealousy, and in whose interests God is pleased so far to interest himself that he takes the violence done to him as done to himself. <hi type="italic">Whoso touches Jacob touches the apple of the eye of Jacob's God.</hi>" So that it is <hi type="italic">crimen læsæ majestatis—high treason,</hi> for which, as for high treason, let Edom expect an ignominious punishment: <hi type="italic">Shame shall cover thee,</hi> and a ruining one; <hi type="italic">thou shalt be cut off for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen20277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20278" type="x-p"/> In the <reference osisRef="Obad.1.12-Obad.1.16">following verses</reference> we are told more particularly, <div eID="gen20278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20279" type="x-p"/> I. What the violence was which Edom did against his brother Jacob, and what are the proofs of this charge. It does not appear that the Edomites did themselves invade Israel, but that was more for want of power than will; they had malice enough to do it, but were not a match for them. But that which is laid to their charge is their barbarous conduct towards Judah and Jerusalem when they were in distress, and ready to be destroyed, probably by the Chaldeans, or upon occasion of some other of the calamities of the Jews; for this seems to have been always their temper towards them. See this charged upon the Edomites (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Ps. cxxxvii. 7</reference>), that <hi type="italic">in the day of Jerusalem they said, Rase it, rase it,</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12">Ezek. xxv. 12</reference>. They are here told particularly what they did, by being told what they should not have done (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.12-Obad.1.14">v. 12-14</reference>): "Thou <hi type="italic">shouldst not have looked,</hi> thou <hi type="italic">shouldst not have entered;</hi> but thou didst so." Note, In reflecting upon ourselves it is good to compare what we have done with what we should have done, our practice with the rule, that we may discover wherein we have done amiss, have <hi type="italic">done those things which we ought not to have done.</hi> We should not have been where we were at such a time, should not have been in such and such company, should not have said what we said, nor have taken the liberty that we took. Sin thus looked upon, in the glass of the commandment, will appear exceedingly sinful. Let us see, <div eID="gen20279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20280" type="x-p"/> 1. What was the case of Judah and Jerusalem when the Edomites behaved themselves thus basely and insulted over them. (1.) It was a day of distress with them (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.12">v. 12</reference>): It was the <hi type="italic">day of their calamity,</hi> so it is called three times, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.13">v. 13</reference>. With the Edomites it was a day of prosperity and peace when with the Israelites it was a day of distress and calamity, for judgment commonly <hi type="italic">begins at the house of God.</hi> Children are corrected when strangers are let alone. (2.) It was the day of <hi type="italic">their destruction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.12">v. 12</reference>), when both city and country were laid waste, were laid <hi type="italic">in ruins.</hi> (3.) It was a day when <hi type="italic">foreigners entered into the gates of Jerusalem,</hi> when the city, after a long siege, was broken up, and the great officers of the king of Babylon's army came, and sat in the gates, as judges of the land; when they cast lots upon the spoils of Jerusalem, as the soldiers on Christ's garments, what shares each of the conquerors shall have, what shares of the lands, what shares of the goods; or they cast lots to determine when and where they should attack it. (4.) It was a day when the <hi type="italic">strangers carried away captive his forces</hi> (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.11">v. 11</reference>), took the men of war prisoners of war, and carried them off, in poverty and shame, to their own country, or such a multitude of captives that they were as an army. (5.) "It was a day when thy brother himself, that had long been at home, at rest in his own land, <hi type="italic">became a stranger,</hi> an exile in a strange land." Now, when this was the woeful case of the Jews, the Edomites, their neighbours and brethren, should have pitied them and helped them, condoled with them and comforted them, and should have trembled to think that their own turn would come next; for, <hi type="italic">if this was done in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?</hi> But, <div eID="gen20280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20281" type="x-p"/> 2. See what was the conduct of the Edomites towards them when they were in this distress, for which they are here condemned. (1.) They looked with pleasure upon the affliction of God's people; they <hi type="italic">stood on the other side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.11">v. 11</reference>), afar off, when they should have come in to the relief of their distressed neighbours, and <hi type="italic">looked upon them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">their day, looked on their affliction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.12-Obad.1.13">v. 12, 13</reference>), with a careless unconcerned eye, as the priest and Levite looked upon the wounded man, and <hi type="italic">passed by on the other side.</hi> Those have a great deal to answer for that are idle spectators of the troubles and afflictions of their neighbours, when they are capable of being their active helpers. But this was not all; they looked upon it with a scornful eye, with an eye of complacency and satisfaction; they looked and laughed to see Israel in distress, saying, <hi type="italic">Aha! so we would have it.</hi> They fed their eyes with the rueful spectacle of Jerusalem's ruin, and looked at it as those that had long looked for it and often wished to see it. Note, We must take heed with what eye we look upon the afflictions of our brethren; and, if we cannot look upon them with a gracious eye of sympathy and tenderness, it is better not to look upon them at all: <hi type="italic">Thou shouldst not have looked</hi> as thou didst <hi type="italic">upon the day of thy brother.</hi> (2.) They triumphed and insulted over them, upbraided their brethren with their sorrows, and made themselves and their companions merry with them. They <hi type="italic">rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction.</hi> They had not the good manners to conceal the pleasure they took in Judah's destruction and to dissemble it, but openly declared it, and rudely and insolently declared it <hi type="italic">to them; they rejoiced over them,</hi> crowed, and hectored, and trampled upon them. Those have the spirit of Edomites that can rejoice over any, especially over Israelites, in the day of their calamity. (3.) They <hi type="italic">spoke proudly-magnified the mouth</hi> (so the word is), against Israel, talked with a great disdain of the suffering Israelites, and with an air of haughtiness of the present safety and prosperity of Edom, as it if might be inferred from their present different state that the tables were turned, and now Esau was beloved, and the favourite of heaven, and Jacob hated and rejected. Note, Those must expect to be in some way or other effectually humbled and mortified themselves that are puffed up and made proud by the humiliations and mortifications of others. (4.) They went further yet, for they <hi type="italic">entered into the gate</hi> of God's people in the day of their calamity, and <hi type="italic">laid hands on their substance.</hi> Though they did not help to conquer them, they helped to plunder them, and put in for a share in the prey, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.13">v. 13</reference>. Jerusalem was thrown open, and then they entered in; its wealth was thrown about, and they seized it for themselves, excusing it with this, that they might as well take it as let it be lost; whereas it was taking what was not their own. Babylon lays Jerusalem waste, but Edom, by meddling with the spoil, becomes <hi type="italic">particeps criminis</hi>—<hi type="italic">partaker of the crime,</hi> and shall be reckoned with as an accessary <hi type="italic">ex post facto</hi>—<hi type="italic">after the fact.</hi> Note, Those do but impoverish themselves that think to enrich themselves by the ruins of the people of God; and those deceive themselves who think they may call all that substance their own which they can lay their hands on in a day of calamity. (5.) They did yet worse things; they not only robbed their brethren, but murdered them, in the day of their calamity; laid hands not only on their substance, but on their persons, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.14">v. 14</reference>. When the victorious sword of the Chaldeans was making bloody work among the Jews many made their escape, and were in a fair way to save themselves by flight; but the Edomites basely intercepted them, <hi type="italic">stood in the cross-way</hi> where several roads met, by each of which the trembling Israelites were making the best of their way from the fury of the pursuers, and there they stopped them: some they barbarously and cowardlike cut off themselves; others they took prisoners, and delivered up to the pursuers, only to ingratiate themselves with them, because they were now the conquerors. They <hi type="italic">should not have been</hi> thus <hi type="italic">cruel</hi> to those that lay at their mercy, and never had done, nor were every likely to do, them any hurt; they should not have betrayed those whom they had such a fair opportunity to protect; but such are the <hi type="italic">tender mercies of the wicked.</hi> One cannot read this without a high degree of compassion towards those who were thus basely abused, who when they fled from the sword of an open enemy, and thought they had got out of the reach of it, fell upon and fell by the sword of a treacherous neighbour, whom they were not apprehensive of any danger from. Nor can one read this without a high degree of indignation towards those who were so perfectly lost to all humanity as to exercise such cruelty upon such proper objects of compassion. (6.) In all this they joined with the open enemies and persecutors of Israel: <hi type="italic">Even thou wast as one of them,</hi> an accessary equally guilty with the principals. He that joins in with the evil doers, and is aiding and abetting in their evil deeds, shall be reckoned, and shall be reckoned with, as one of them. <div eID="gen20281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20282" type="x-p"/> II. What the shame is that shall cover them for this violence of theirs. 1. They shall soon find that the cup is going round, even the cup of trembling; and, when they come to be in the same calamitous condition that the Israel of God is now in, they will be ashamed to remember how they triumphed over them (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">The day of the Lord is near upon all the heathen,</hi> when God will recompense tribulation to the troublers of his church. Though judgment begin at the house of God, it shall not end there. This should effectually restrain us from triumphing over others in their misery, that we know not how soon it may be our own case. 2. Their enmity to the people of God, and the injuries they had done them, shall be recompensed into their own bosoms: <hi type="italic">As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee.</hi> The righteous God will render both to nations and to particular persons <hi type="italic">according to their works;</hi> and the punishment is often made exactly to answer to the sin, and those that have abused others come to be themselves abused in like manner. The just and jealous God will find out a time and way to avenge the wrongs done to his people on those that have been injurious to them. <hi type="italic">As you have drunk upon my holy mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.16">v. 16</reference>), that is, as God's professing people, who inhabit his holy mountain, have drunk deeply of the cup of affliction (and their being of the holy mountain would not excuse them), <hi type="italic">so shall all the heathen drink,</hi> in their turn, of the same bitter cup; for, if God <hi type="italic">bring evil on the city that is called by his name, shall those be unpunished</hi> that never knew his name? See <reference osisRef="Jer.25.29">Jer. xxv. 29</reference>. And it is part of the burden of Edom (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">Jer. xlix. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Those whose judgment was not to drink of the cup</hi> (who had reason to promise themselves an exemption from it) have assuredly drunken, and <hi type="italic">shall Edom</hi> that is the generation of God's wrath <hi type="italic">go unpunished?</hi> No, <hi type="italic">thou shalt surely drink of it;</hi> the <hi type="italic">cup of trembling shall be taken out of the hand</hi> of God's people, and put <hi type="italic">into the hand of those that afflict them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.22-Isa.51.23">Isa. li. 22, 23</reference>. Nay, they may expect their case to be worse in the day of their distress than that of Israel was in their day; for, (1.) The afflictions of God's people were but for a moment, and soon had an end, but their enemies shall <hi type="italic">drink continually</hi> the <hi type="italic">wine of God's wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Rev. xiv. 10</reference>. (2.) The dregs of the cup are reserved for the <hi type="italic">wicked of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Ps. lxxv. 8</reference>); they shall <hi type="italic">drink and swallow down,</hi> or <hi type="italic">sup up</hi> (as the margin reads it), shall drink it to the bottom. (3.) The people of God, though they may be made to drink of the wine of astonishment for a while (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.3">Ps. lx. 3</reference>), shall yet recover, and come to themselves again; but the heathen shall drink and be <hi type="italic">as though they had not been;</hi> there shall be neither any remains nor any remembrance of them, but they shall be wholly extirpated and rooted out. <hi type="italic">So let all thy enemies perish, O Lord!</hi> so they shall perish, if they turn not.
entries.7f7c045a1b7e0eb730687f1eb856b9e6472d64be: <div eID="gen20282" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises to Israel and Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen20283" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> But upon mount Zion shall be deliverance, and there shall be holiness; and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau for stubble, and they shall kindle in them, and devour them; and there shall not be <hi type="italic">any</hi> remaining of the house of Esau; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> And <hi type="italic">they of</hi> the south shall possess the mount of Esau; and <hi type="italic">they of</hi> the plain the Philistines: and they shall possess the fields of Ephraim, and the fields of Samaria: and Benjamin <hi type="italic">shall possess</hi> Gilead. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the captivity of this host of the children of Israel <hi type="italic">shall possess</hi> that of the Canaanites, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Zarephath; and the captivity of Jerusalem, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Sepharad, shall possess the cities of the south. <hi type="super">21</hi> And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's. <div eID="gen20283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20284" type="x-p"/> After the destruction of the church's enemies is threatened, which will be completely accomplished in the great day of recompence, and that judgment for which Christ came once, and will come again, into this world, here follow precious promises of the salvation of the church, with which this prophecy concludes, and those of Joel and Amos did, which, however they might be in part fulfilled in the return of the Jews out of Babylon notwithstanding the triumphs of Edom in their captivity, as if it were perpetual, are yet, doubtless, to have their full accomplishment in that great salvation wrought out by Jesus Christ, to which all the prophets bore witness. It is promised here, <div eID="gen20284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20285" type="x-p"/> I. That there shall be salvation upon Mount Zion, that holy hill where God sets his anointed King (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Upon Mount Zion shall be deliverance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Obad.1.17">v. 17</reference>. There shall be <hi type="italic">those that escape;</hi> so the margin. A remnant of Israel, <hi type="italic">upon the holy mountain</hi> shall be saved, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.16">v. 16</reference>. Christ said, <hi type="italic">Salvation is of the Jews,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.22">John iv. 22</reference>. God wrought deliverances for the Jews, typical of our redemption by Christ. But Mount Zion is the gospel-church, from which the New-Testament law <hi type="italic">went forth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>. There salvation shall be preached and prayed for; to the gospel-church those are added who <hi type="italic">shall be saved;</hi> and for those who come in faith and hope to this Mount Zion deliverance shall be wrought from wrath and the curse, from sin, and death, and hell, while those who continue afar off shall be left to perish. <div eID="gen20285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20286" type="x-p"/> II. That, where there is salvation, there shall be sanctification in order to it: <hi type="italic">And there shall be holiness,</hi> to prepare and qualify the children of Zion for this deliverance; for wherever God designs glory he gives grace. Temporal deliverances are indeed wrought for us in mercy when with them there is holiness, when there is wrought in us a disposition to receive them with love and gratitude to God; when we are sanctified, they are sanctified to us. Holiness is itself a great deliverance, and an earnest of that eternal salvation which we look for. <hi type="italic">There,</hi> upon Mount Zion, in the gospel-church, <hi type="italic">shall be holiness;</hi> for that is it which <hi type="italic">becomes God's house for ever,</hi> and the great design of the gospel, and its grace, is to plant and promote holiness. There shall be the Holy Spirit, the holy ordinances, the holy Jesus, and a select remnant of holy souls, in whom, and among whom, the holy God will delight to dwell. Note, Where there is holiness there shall be deliverance. <div eID="gen20286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20287" type="x-p"/> III. That this salvation and sanctification shall spread, and prevail, and get ground in the world: The <hi type="italic">house of Jacob,</hi> even this <hi type="italic">Mount Zion,</hi> with the deliverance and their holiness there wrought, shall <hi type="italic">possess their possessions;</hi> that is, the gospel-church shall be set up among the heathen, and shall replenish the earth; the apostles of Christ by their preaching shall gain possession of the hearts of men for him whose messengers and ministers they are, and when they possess their hearts they shall <hi type="italic">possess their possessions,</hi> for those who have given up themselves to the Lord give up all they have to him. When Lydia's heart was opened to Christ her house was opened to his ministers. When the Gentile nations became <hi type="italic">nations of those that were saved,</hi> were disciplined, <hi type="italic">walked in the light</hi> of the Lord, and <hi type="italic">brought their glory and honour into the new Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.24">Rev. xxi. 24</reference>), then the <hi type="italic">house of Jacob possessed their possessions.</hi> This is the part fulfilled by the planting of the Christian religion in the world, and shall be fulfilled yet more and more by the setting up of Christ's throne where Satan's seat is, and the erecting of trophies of his victory upon the ruins of the devil's kingdom. Now here is foretold, <div eID="gen20287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20288" type="x-p"/> 1. How this possession shall be <hi type="italic">gained,</hi> and the opposition given to it got over (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame,</hi> for their God is, and will be, a <hi type="italic">consuming fire;</hi> and the house of Esau shall be for <hi type="italic">stubble,</hi> easily devoured and consumed by this fire. This is fulfilled, (1.) In the conversion of multitudes by the grace of Christ; the gospel, preached in the house of Jacob and Joseph, and there owned and professed, shall be as a fire and a flame to melt and to soften hard hearts, to burn up the dross of sin and corruption, that they may be purified and refined with the <hi type="italic">spirit of judgment and</hi> the <hi type="italic">spirit of burning.</hi> Christ, when he comes, shall be <hi type="italic">as a refiner's fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1-Mal.3.2">Mal. iii. 1, 2</reference>. (2.) In the confusion of all the impenitent implacable enemies of the gospel of Christ, that oppose it and do all they can to hinder the setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah by it. The gospel day is a day that <hi type="italic">burns like an oven,</hi> in which <hi type="italic">all the proud, and all that do wickedly, shall be a stubble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal. iv. 1</reference>. Jacob and Joseph shall be as a fire and a flame; for those that meddle with them, to do them hurt, will find that they do so at their peril; they shall be to them as <hi type="italic">a torch of fire in a sheaf,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.6">Zech. xii. 6</reference>. The word of God in the mouth of his ministers is said to be like fire, and the people as wood to be devoured by it, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.14">Jer. v. 14</reference>. And the <hi type="italic">man of sin</hi> is to be <hi type="italic">consumed by the breath of Christ's mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2 Thess. ii. 8</reference>. Those that are not refined as gold by fire of the gospel shall be consumed as dross by it; for it will be a savour either of life or of death. When idols and idolatry were abolished, and the wealth and power of nations were brought into the service of Christ and his gospel, and the spoils of the <hi type="italic">strong man armed</hi> were divided by him that was <hi type="italic">stronger than he,</hi> then the house of Jacob and Joseph devoured <hi type="italic">the house of Esau,</hi> so that there was none of them left remaining. This the Lord <hi type="italic">spoke</hi> by his prophets, and this he did by his apostles. <div eID="gen20288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20289" type="x-p"/> 2. How far this possession shall extend, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.19-Obad.1.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. This is described in Jewish language, which speaks the accession made to the land of Israel, after the return out of captivity into Babylon. The <hi type="italic">captivity of this host of Israel,</hi> that is, this host of Israel that have been so long in captivity and now they have come back are still called the <hi type="italic">children of the captivity,</hi> these shall not only recover their own land, but shall gain ground upon their neighbours adjoining to them, some of whom shall become proselytes and shall incorporate with the Jews, who, by possessing them in a holy communion, possess their land. We must reckon ourselves truly enriched by the conversion of our neighbours to the fear of God and the faith of Christ, and their coming to join with us in the worship of God. Such an accession to our Christian communion we must reckon to be more our wealth and strength than an accession to our estates. Or, The ancient inhabitants of those lands that were carried away into captivity being lost, and never returning to their estates, the children of Israel shall take possession of that which lies next them; for their numbers shall so increase that their own land shall be too strait for them, and their neighbours' estates shall escheat to them <hi type="italic">ob defectum sanguinis—through default of heirs.</hi> They shall enter upon that which is adjoining to them. The country of Esau shall be possessed by those <hi type="italic">of the south</hi> parts of Canaan, for to them it lies contiguous. Those <hi type="italic">of the plain,</hi> on the <hi type="italic">west</hi> of Canaan, which was a champaign country, shall enter upon <hi type="italic">the land of the Philistines,</hi> their neighbours. Those of Judah, which was the chief of the two returning tribes, shall possess <hi type="italic">the field of Ephraim and Samaria,</hi> which before belonged to the ten tribes; and Benjamin, the other tribe, shall possess Gilead on the other side of Jordan, which had belonged to the two tribes and a half. The kingdom of Israel shall join with that of Judah both in civil and sacred interests, and, as friends and brethren, shall mutually possess and enjoy one another; and both together shall <hi type="italic">possess the Canaanites,</hi> even to Zarephath, which <hi type="italic">belongeth to Zidon;</hi> and Jerusalem shall possess the <hi type="italic">cities of the south,</hi> even to Sepharad. Thus did the Jews enlarge their borders on all sides. The modern rabbin teach their scholars by Zarephath and Sepharad to understand France and Spain, grounding upon this a foolish groundless expectation that some time or other the Jews shall be masters of those countries; and they call and count the Christians <hi type="italic">Edomites,</hi> over whom they are to have dominion. But the promise here, no doubt, has a spiritual signification, and had its accomplishment in the setting up of the Christian church, the gospel-Israel, in the world, and shall have its accomplishment more and more in the enlargement of it and the additions made to it, till the mystical body is completed. When ministers and Christians prevail with their neighbours to come to Christ, to yield themselves to the Lord, they possess them. The converts that Abraham had are said to be the <hi type="italic">souls that he had gotten,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.12.5">Gen. xii. 5</reference>. The possession is gained, not <hi type="italic">vi et armis—by force and arms;</hi> for the <hi type="italic">weapons of our warfare are not carnal,</hi> but <hi type="italic">spiritual;</hi> it is by the preaching of the gospel, and the power of divine grace going along with it, that this possession is got and kept. <div eID="gen20289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20290" type="x-p"/> IV. That the kingdom of the Redeemer shall be erected and maintained, to the comfort of his loyal subjects and the terror and shame of all his enemies (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">The kingdom shall be the Lord's,</hi> the Lord Christ's. God shall give it to him, by putting all things into his hand, all power both in heaven and in earth; men shall give it to him, by resigning themselves to him as his willing people, and appointing him their head. Now the work of kings is to protect their subjects and suppress their enemies; and this Christ will do; he will both reward and punish. 1. The mountain of Zion shall be saved; on it <hi type="italic">saviours</hi> shall <hi type="italic">come,</hi> the preachers of the gospel, who are called saviours, because their business is to save themselves and those that hear them; and in this they are <hi type="italic">workers together with Christ,</hi> but to little purpose if he by his grace did not <hi type="italic">work together with them.</hi> 2. The mountain of Esau shall be judged; and the same that come as saviours on Mount Zion shall <hi type="italic">judge</hi> the <hi type="italic">mountain of Esau;</hi> for the word of the gospel in their mouth, that saves believers, judges unbelievers, convinces and condemns them. Christ's ministers are <hi type="italic">saviours on Mount Zion</hi> when they preach that he <hi type="italic">that believes shall be saved;</hi> but they judge the mount of Esau when they preach <hi type="italic">that he that believeth not shall be damned,</hi> which they are not only commissioned, but commanded to do, <reference osisRef="Mark.16.16">Mark xvi. 16</reference>. And in the course of God's providence his scripture is fulfilled; when God raises up friends to the church in her distress (as he <hi type="italic">raised up judges</hi> to deliver Israel of old, <reference osisRef="Judg.2.16">Judg. ii. 16</reference>), then <hi type="italic">saviours come on Mount Zion,</hi> to save it from being sunk and ruined; and when the enemies of the church are brought down, and their power broken, then is the <hi type="italic">mount of Esau judged;</hi> and this shall be done in every age in such a way as God thinks best; we may depend upon it that the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church, but the church shall prevail against them; <hi type="italic">for the kingdom shall be the Lord's;</hi> the kingdoms of the world shall become his, and he has taken, and will take, to himself his great power and reign.  <chapter eID="Obad.1"/> <div eID="gen20290" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen20261" osisID="Obad" type="book"/>

entries.c7a8caf981dd15f91471f68f0cab3be7219961f2: <chapter n="1" osisID="Obad.1" sID="Obad.1"/> <chapter eID="Obad.1"/> <div eID="gen23355" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="1" osisID="Obad.1" sID="Obad.1"/> <div sID="gen23356" type="introduction"/>
entries.5029fa0ebbca158f3dd5adede4b7ef6b0ed4241a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12648"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23357" type="x-p"/> This is the shortest book in the Old Testament. The name means "servant of Jehovah." Obadiah stands fourth among the minor prophets according to the Hebrew arrangement of the canon, the fifth according to the Greek. Some consider him to be the same as the Obadiah who superintended the restoration of the temple under Josiah, 627 B.C. (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.12">2Ch 34:12</reference>). But Ob 11-16, 20 imply that Jerusalem was by this time overthrown by the Chaldeans, and that he refers to the cruelty of Edom towards the Jews on that occasion, which is referred to also in <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">22</reference>; Eze 25:12-14; 35:1-15; <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>. From comparing Ob 5 with <reference osisRef="Jer.49.9">Jr 49:9</reference>, Ob 6 with <reference osisRef="Jer.49.10">Jr 49:10</reference>, Ob 8 with <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jr 49:7</reference>, it appears that Jeremiah embodied in his prophecies part of Obadiah's, as he had done in the case of other prophets also (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1-Isa.16.14">Is 15:1-16:14</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1-Jer.48.47">Jr 48:1-47</reference>). The reason for the present position of Obadiah before other of the minor prophets anterior in date is: Amos at the close of his prophecies foretells the subjugation of Edom hereafter by the Jews; the arranger of the minor prophets in one volume, therefore, placed Obadiah next, as being a fuller statement, and, as it were, a commentary on the foregoing briefer prophecy of Amos as to Edom [Maurer]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>). The date of Obadiah's prophecies was probably immediately after the taking of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, 588 B.C. Five years afterwards (583 B.C.) Edom was conquered by Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah must have incorporated part of Obadiah's prophecies with his own immediately after they were uttered, thus stamping his canonicity.<div eID="gen23357" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23356" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23358" type="x-p"/> Jerome makes him contemporary with Hosea, Joel, and Amos. It is an argument in favor of this view that Jeremiah would be more likely to insert in his prophecies a portion from a preceding prophet than from a contemporary. If so, the allusion in Ob 11-14 will be to one of the former captures of Jerusalem: by the Egyptians under Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.25">1Ki 14:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.2">2Ch 12:2</reference>, &c.), or that by the Philistines and Arabians in the reign of Joram (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.16">2Ch 21:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.17">17</reference>); or that by Joash, king of Israel, in the reign of Amaziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.22">2Ch 25:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.23">23</reference>); or that in the reign of Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1">2Ki 24:1</reference>, &c.); or that in the reign of Jehoiachin (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8-2Kgs.24.16">2Ki 24:8-16</reference>). On all occasions the Idumeans were hostile to the Jews; and the terms in which that enmity is characterized are not stronger in Obadiah than in <reference osisRef="Joel.3.19">Joe 3:19</reference> (compare Ob 10); <reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>. The probable capture of Jerusalem alluded to by Obadiah is that by Joash and the Israelites in the reign of Amaziah. For as, a little before, in the reign of the same Amaziah, the Jews had treated harshly the Edomites after conquering them in battle (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.11-2Chr.25.23">2Ch 25:11-23</reference>), it is probable that the Edomites, in revenge, joined the Israelites in the attack on Jerusalem [Jaeger].<div eID="gen23358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23359" type="x-p"/> This book may be divided into two parts: (1) Ob 1-6 set forth Edom's violence toward his brother Israel in the day of the latter's distress, and his coming destruction with the rest of the foes of Judah; (2) Ob 17-21, the coming re-establishment of the Jews in their own possessions, to which shall be added those of the neighboring peoples, and especially those of Edom.<div eID="gen23359" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <div sID="gen23360" type="x-p"/> Ob 1-21. Doom of Edom for Cruelty to Judah, Edom's Brother; Restoration of the Jews.<div eID="gen23360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12648"/><hi type="bold">1. Obadiah--</hi>that is, servant of Jehovah; same as Abdeel and Arabic Abd-allah.<div eID="gen23361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We--</hi>I and my people.<div eID="gen23362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Is 21:10</reference>).<div eID="gen23363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and an ambassador is sent--</hi>Yea, an ambassador is already sent, namely, an angel, to stir up the Assyrians (and afterwards the Chaldeans) against Edom. The result of the ambassador's message on the heathen is, they simultaneously exclaim, "Arise ye, and let us (with united strength) rise," &c. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.14">Jr 49:14</reference> quotes this. <div eID="gen23364" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a54c70230964fc5c9f3b325248a996597defb6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12649"/><div sID="gen23365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12649"/><hi type="bold">2. I have made thee small--</hi>Thy reduction to insignificance is as sure as if it were already accomplished; therefore the past tense is used [Maurer]. Edom then extended from Dedan of Arabia to Bozrah in the north (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.8">Jr 49:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.13">13</reference>). Calvin explains it, "Whereas thou wast made by Me an insignificant people, why art thou so proud" (Ob 3)? But if so, why should the heathen peoples be needed to subdue one so insignificant? <reference osisRef="Jer.49.15">Jr 49:15</reference>, confirms Maurer's view. <div eID="gen23365" type="x-p"/>
entries.6420772f143ffd8902e7d83ae708e1eae5eaa8a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12650"/><div sID="gen23366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12650"/><hi type="bold">3. clefts of ... rock--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.2.14">So 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.28">Jr 48:28</reference>). The cities of Edom, and among them Petra (Hebrew, sela, meaning "rock," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">2Ki 14:7</reference>, Margin), the capital, in the Wady Musa, consisted of houses mostly cut in the rocks. <div eID="gen23366" type="x-p"/>
entries.22f9e76b503ebcf576ced575c0a8e12cf6a38e9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12651"/><div sID="gen23367" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12651"/><hi type="bold">4. exalt thyself--</hi>or supply from the second clause, "thy nest" [Maurer] (Compare <reference osisRef="Job.20.6">Job 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.16">Jr 49:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.2">Am 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set ... nest among ... stars--</hi>namely, on the loftiest hills which seem to reach the very stars. Edom is a type of Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.10">Da 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.37">11:37</reference>).<div eID="gen23368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thence will I bring thee down--</hi>in spite of thy boast (Ob 3), "Who shall bring me down?" <div eID="gen23369" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1abf4eb0f403d314f6ed066ee3164b8f54c1704: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12652"/><div sID="gen23370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12652"/><hi type="bold">5. The spoliation which thou shalt suffer shall not be such as that which thieves cause, bad as that is, for these when they have seized enough, or all they can get in a hurry, leave the rest--</hi>nor such as grape-gatherers cause in a vineyard, for they, when they have gathered most of the grapes, leave gleanings behind--but it shall be utter, so as to leave thee nothing. The exclamation, "How art thou cut off!" bursting in amidst the words of the image, marks strongly excited feeling. The contrast between Edom where no gleanings shall be left, and Israel where at the worst a gleaning is left (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Is 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.13">24:13</reference>), is striking. <div eID="gen23370" type="x-p"/>
entries.51d7f347ff472e240a32a2d56ebf686c0eea5eea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12653"/><div sID="gen23371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12653"/><hi type="bold">6. How are the things of Esau searched out!--</hi>by hostile soldiers seeking booty. Compare with Ob 5, 6 here, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.9">Jr 49:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.10">10</reference>.<div eID="gen23371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hidden things--</hi>or "places." Edom abounded in such hiding-places, as caves, clefts in the rock, &c. None of these would be left unexplored by the foe. <div eID="gen23372" type="x-p"/>
entries.170a877652d94a4ad0fccd588712626f8d1c23f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12654"/><div sID="gen23373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12654"/><hi type="bold">7. Men of thy confederacy--</hi>that is, thy confederates.<div eID="gen23373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought thee ... to the border--</hi>that is, when Idumean ambassadors shall go to confederate states seeking aid, these latter shall conduct them with due ceremony to their border, giving them empty compliments, but not the aid required [Drusius]. This view agrees with the context, which speaks of false friends deceiving Edom: that is, failing to give help in need (compare <reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job 6:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.15">15</reference>). Calvin translates, "have driven," that is, shall drive thee; shall help to drive thee to thy border on thy way into captivity in foreign lands.<div eID="gen23374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the men that were at peace with thee--</hi>literally, "the men of thy peace." Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.22">Jr 38:22</reference>, Margin, where also the same formula occurs, "prevailed against thee."<div eID="gen23375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they that eat thy bread--</hi>the poorer tribes of the desert who subsisted on the bounty of Edom. Compare again <reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>, which seems to have been before Obadiah's mind, as his words were before Jeremiah's.<div eID="gen23376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have laid a wound under thee--</hi>"laid" implies that their intimacy was used as a SNARE laid with a view to wound; also, these guest friends of Edom, instead of the cushions ordinarily laid under guests at table, laid snares to wound, that is, had a secret understanding with Edom's foe for that purpose. Maurer translates, "a snare." But English Version agrees with the Hebrew, which means, literally, "a bandage for a wound."<div eID="gen23377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none understanding--</hi>none of the wisdom for which Edom was famed (see Ob 8) to extricate him from his perilous position.<div eID="gen23378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in him--</hi>instead of "in thee." The change implies the alienation of God from Edom: Edom has so estranged himself from God, that He speaks now of him, not to him. <div eID="gen23379" type="x-p"/>
entries.567cbab34525fd9d2dd2b7287c9b764a459a98f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12655"/><div sID="gen23380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12655"/>8. (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">Is 49:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.5.12">Job 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.5.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Is 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">Jr 19:7</reference>).<div eID="gen23380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in that day ... even destroy--</hi>Heretofore Edom, through its intercourse with Babylon and Egypt, and from its means of information through the many caravans passing to and fro between Europe and India, has been famed for knowledge; but in that day at last ("even") I will destroy its wise men.<div eID="gen23381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mount of Esau--</hi>that is, Idumea, which was a mountainous region. <div eID="gen23382" type="x-p"/>
entries.51e526e098ff718363aa13017901fde9bae97cad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12656"/><div sID="gen23383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12656"/><hi type="bold">9. cut off by slaughter--</hi>Maurer translates, "on account of the slaughter," namely, that inflicted on Judea by Edom (compare Ob 14). The Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate connect these words with Ob 10, "for the slaughter, for the violence (of which thou art guilty) against thy brother Jacob." English Version, "cut off by slaughter" (that is, an utter cutting off), answers well to "cut off for ever" (Ob 10). However, the arrangement of the Septuagint gives a better parallelism in Ob 10. "For the slaughter" (1) being balanced in just retribution by "thou shalt be cut off for ever" (4); as "For thy violence (not so bad as slaughter) against thy brother Jacob" (2) is balanced by "shame (not so bad as being cut off) shall cover thee" (3). Shame and extinction shall repay violence and slaughter (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.52">Mt 26:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Re 13:10</reference>). Compare as to Edom's violence, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12">Eze 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>. <div eID="gen23383" type="x-p"/>
entries.85bf3b7c65d73542a8540ad8ed716c1539a2223b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12657"/><div sID="gen23384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12657"/><hi type="bold">10. against thy brother--</hi>This aggravates the sin of Esau, that it was against him who was his brother by birth and by circumcision. The posterity of Esau followed in the steps of their father's hatred to Jacob by violence against Jacob's seed (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.41">Ge 27:41</reference>).<div eID="gen23384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jacob--</hi>not merely his own brother, but his twin brother; hence the name Jacob, not Israel, is here put emphatically. Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.23.7">De 23:7</reference> for the opposite feeling which Jacob's seed was commanded to entertain towards Edom's.<div eID="gen23385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shame ... cover thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.35.26">Psa 35:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.7">69:7</reference>).<div eID="gen23386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23387" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.34.10">Is 34:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.9">Eze 35:9</reference>; Mal 1:4). Idumea, as a nation, should be "cut off for ever," though the land should be again inhabited. <div eID="gen23387" type="x-p"/>
entries.9621f6f51acd9a96b8ca75dc33005482c0068d3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12658"/><div sID="gen23388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12658"/><hi type="bold">11. thou stoodest on the other side--</hi>in an attitude of hostility, rather than the sympathy which became a brother, feasting thine eyes (see Ob 12) with the misery of Jacob, and eagerly watching for his destruction. So Messiah, the antitype to Jerusalem, abandoned by His kinsmen (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">Psa 38:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strangers--</hi>the Philistines, Arabians in the reign of Jehoram, &c. (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.16">2Ch 21:16</reference>); the Syrians in the reign of Joash of Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.24">2Ch 24:24</reference>); the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.1-2Chr.36.23">2Ch 36:1-23</reference>).<div eID="gen23389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carried ... captive his forces--</hi>his "host" (Ob 20): the multitude of Jerusalem's inhabitants.<div eID="gen23390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast lots upon Jerusalem--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Joel.3.3">Joe 3:3</reference>). So Messiah, Jerusalem's antitype, had lots cast for His only earthly possessions (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.18">Psa 22:18</reference>). <div eID="gen23391" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8319285e181776650eb3b2c5d6938726eefc07b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12659"/><div sID="gen23392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12659"/><hi type="bold">12. looked on--</hi>with malignant pleasure, and a brutal stare. So the antitypes, Messiah's foes (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.17">Psa 22:17</reference>). Maurer translates, as the Margin, "thou shouldest not look" any more. English Version agrees with the context better.<div eID="gen23392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day of thy brother--</hi>his day of calamity.<div eID="gen23393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">became a stranger--</hi>that is, was banished as an alien from his own land. God sends heavy calamities on those who rejoice in the calamities of their enemies (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.5">Pr 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.17">24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.18">18</reference>). Contrast the opposite conduct of David and of the divine Son of David in a like case (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.13-Ps.35.15">Psa 35:13-15</reference>).<div eID="gen23394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spoken proudly--</hi>literally, "made great the mouth"; proudly insulting the fallen (<reference osisRef="Ezek.35.13">Eze 35:13</reference>, Margin; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.6">Re 13:6</reference>). <div eID="gen23395" type="x-p"/>
entries.8df88174a9decb1c2b4b16e4641259a25de5f662: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12660"/><div sID="gen23396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12660"/><hi type="bold">13. substance--</hi>translated "forces" in Ob 11. <div eID="gen23396" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ca71321886943efc82b99384da2d4bc388c9d9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12661"/><div sID="gen23397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12661"/><hi type="bold">14. stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his--</hi>Judah's.<div eID="gen23397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that did escape--</hi>The Jews naturally fled by the crossways. (Maurer translates, "narrow mountain passes") well known to them, to escape to the desert, and through Edom to Egypt; but the Edomites stood ready to intercept the fugitives and either kill or "deliver them up" to the foe. <div eID="gen23398" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd328d08807d09937d9d575f84a9e9510689cf07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12662"/><div sID="gen23399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12662"/><hi type="bold">15. For--</hi>resumptive in connection with Ob 10, wherein Edom was threatened with cutting off for ever.<div eID="gen23399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day of the Lord--</hi>the day in which He will manifest Himself as the Righteous Punisher of the ungodly peoples (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.14">Joe 3:14</reference>). The "all" shows that the fulfilment is not exhausted in the punishment inflicted on the surrounding nations by the instrumentality of Nebuchadnezzar; but, as in <reference osisRef="Joel.3.14">Joe 3:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Zech.12.3">Zec 12:3</reference>, that the last judgment to come on the nations confederate against Jerusalem is referred to.<div eID="gen23400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee--</hi>the righteous principle of retribution in kind (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.17">Le 24:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.2">Mt 7:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Judg.1.6">Jud 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>; 8:19; <reference osisRef="Esth.7.10">Es 7:10</reference>).<div eID="gen23401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy reward--</hi>the reward of thy deed (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9-Isa.3.11">Is 3:9-11</reference>). <div eID="gen23402" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb3340f50243db1eb9960a4e7ff737f352a1d980: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12663"/><div sID="gen23403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12663"/><hi type="bold">16. ye ... upon my holy mountain--</hi>a periphrasis for, "ye Jews" [Maurer], whom Obadiah now by a sudden apostrophe addresses. The clause, "upon My holy mountain," expresses the reason of the vengeance to be taken on Judah's foes; namely, that Jerusalem is God's holy mountain, the seat of His temple, and Judah His covenant-people. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">Jr 49:12</reference>, which is copied from Obadiah, establishes this view (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>).<div eID="gen23403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ye have drunk, &c.--</hi>namely, the cup of wrath, being dispossessed of your goods and places as a nation, by Edom and all the heathen; so shall all the heathen (Edom included) drink the same cup (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.3">Psa 60:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Is 51:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.12">Jr 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.33">25:15-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">49:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.7">51:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">22</reference> <reference osisRef="Nah.3.11">Na 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.16">Ha 2:16</reference>).<div eID="gen23404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continually--</hi>whereas Judah's calamity shall be temporary (Ob 17). The foes of Judah shall never regain their former position (Ob 18, 19).<div eID="gen23405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swallow down--</hi>so as not to leave anything in the cup of calamity; not merely "drink" (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Psa 75:8</reference>).<div eID="gen23406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be as though they had not been--</hi>not a trace left of their national existence (<reference osisRef="Job.10.19">Job 10:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">Psa 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.21">Eze 26:21</reference>). <div eID="gen23407" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad8ccabadb5fee658eef53ee69cf077e983cb2dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12664"/><div sID="gen23408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12664"/><hi type="bold">17. upon ... Zion ... deliverance--</hi>both in the literal sense and spiritual sense (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.32">Joe 2:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.13">Is 46:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.20">59:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>). Maurer as the Margin explains it, "there shall be a remnant that shall escape." Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.37.32">Is 37:32</reference>; to the deliverance from Sennacherib there described Grotius thinks Obadiah here refers. "Jerusalem shall not be taken, and many of the neighboring peoples also shall find deliverance there."
